mainVideo.title: Let’s Learn English - Level 2 -  Lesson 1: Budget Cuts

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Hum. Oh! “Important meeting. Everyone must come.” Well, back to work! And my boss has called a meeting. I wonder what it's about. Maybe we're all getting raises! Ooo, there's Jonathan! Maybe he knows. Professor Bot: Hi! I'm Professor Bot! This video is all about work. People talk about jobs and things that happen at work. Your assignment is to find as many work words as you can. Don't worry, I'll help. Anna: So, Jonathan, what do you think today's meeting is about? The email sounded important. Jonathan: Well, I have heard people in the building talking about budget cuts. Anna: Oh! Budget cuts? Wait, who has been talking about budget cuts? Jonathan: Mark in Accounting. Anna: Mark in Accounting? That's one person. That's not “people.” Jonathan: I know, but Mark knows everything that goes on at The Studio. Anna: That is true. But wait, look at us. We shouldn't gossip. That's how rumors start. We'll just go to the meeting and see what happens. Jonathan: You're right. No more talk about budget cuts. Amelia: Budget cuts? Oh no! Amelia: I just heard Anna and Jonathan talking about budget cuts. Kaveh: That must be what the meeting is about. When there are budget cuts, people lose their jobs. Amelia: Not you. You're a good reporter. Kaveh: And it's not you. You've done a great job as a videographer. Amelia: I can't go back to being a detective. Criminals scare me! Kaveh: And I can't go back to being a teacher! High school kids scare me! Professor Bot: Did you hear any work words? They talked about a lot of jobs. You can make the name of a job by adding an ending to a verb! Kaveh reports, so, he's a reporter. Amelia used to detect, so she was a detective. If you teach, you're a teacher. And a videographer….uh, I think you understand. Back to the story. Kaveh: Penelope, have you heard the news? Today's meeting is about budget cuts. Penelope: That's awful! What should I do? Kaveh: Update your résumé. I’ve already updated mine. I’ll see you at the meeting. Ms. Weaver: Hello everyone! Quiet, please. Quiet, please! Ms. Weaver: This meeting won’t take long. Then you can all leave. Ms. Weaver: What is wrong with everyone? You look like I'm going to fire you. Ha-ha-ha-ha-ha! Seriously, what is wrong with everyone? Anna: Excuse me, Ms. Weaver? Ms. Weaver: Yes, Anna. Anna: Well, everyone has been worrying about, you know … We’ve been worrying that you are going to fire us! Ms. Weaver: I’m not going to fire any of you! No! The reason for this meeting is to tell you what a good job you’ve been doing and give out new assignments. Budget cuts have been happening. But only one person has lost their job -- Mark in Accounting? Now, let’s talk about those new assignments. Professor Bot: Ms. Weaver's team is doing a good job! How did you do? Did you find all of the work words? Here's a list you can check.
boss meeting raises email budget cuts Accounting gossip rumors lose reporter résumé videographer detective teacher update fire assignment

mainVideo.title: Let’s Learn English - Level 2 - Lesson 2: The Interview

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Ms. Weaver is giving new assignments out. I am ready to take on anything she gives me. Well, except reporting traffic from a helicopter. Wish me luck. Professor Bot: I wonder what Anna’s new assignment will be? Professor Bot here! While you are watching, look for phrasal, or two-word verbs. Some stay together, like “go back” and some can come apart, like “give [assignments] out.” Good luck, Anna! Ms. Weaver: So, as I said at the meeting last week, I have new assignments for everyone at The Studio. Anna, you're good at asking questions. So, I want you to go back to hosting and reporting. Anna: That sounds great. Ms. Weaver: You're also a team player. So, I want you team up with someone ... Anna: That sounds even better! Ms. Weaver: ... someone who is very "different" from you. Anna: That sounds ... what do you mean "different"? Ms. Weaver: Well, you are very cheerful, you're a people person. I want you to team up with someone who ... isn't. Anna: Ms. Weaver, I will find that person. Mimi: Excuse me. Are you using this chair? Pete: Yes. Anna: Pete, hi! Thanks for meeting me. Pete: Sure. But I don’t have lots of time, Anna. I’m busy looking for work. Anna: Pete, you can tear these want ads up and throw them away! I have good news! Pete: Anna, I was working on that crossword puzzle. Anna: Oh. Sorry. Sorry. Pete, forget about the crossword puzzle. I have a job offer for you! Pete: I'm listening. Anna: My boss wants me to team up with someone to host a talk show. But the person must be different from me. So, I thought of you. Pete: Different from you? What do you mean? Anna: I'm sorry, Pete, I don't have time right now. Here's my boss's address. Your interview is tomorrow morning at 10 am. Pete: But what do you mean “different”? Anna: Just be yourself, Pete. Just be yourself. Professor Bot: Did you find any two-word verbs? Here’s one example. Pete can throw the want ads away! Throw away is a two-word verb. Ms. Weaver: Thanks for coming in, Pete. Pete: Thanks for the opportunity, Ms. Weaver. Ms. Weaver: I need to find out if you have the skills for this job. And I want you to be completely honest. Pete: Okay. Ms. Weaver: First, let's talk about your personal skills. Pete, are you a people person? Pete: Well, okay, sometimes I think people talk too much. Ms. Weaver: Pete, what work of yours are you most proud of? Pete: Last year, I locked myself in a cabin and wrote a book. I didn't speak to anybody the entire time! It was the best two months of my life. Ms. Weaver: Okay. I think I’ve heard enough. Anna: Hey! Hey, Pete, how was the interview with Ms. Weaver? Pete: Well, she said I was grumpy and not good with people. Anna: And … ? Pete: And, I got the job! Anna: I knew it! Congratulations! Let's go celebrate. Pete: Okay! Professor Bot: Did you find more two-word verbs? mainVideo.title: Let’s Learn English - Level 2 - Lesson 3: He Said - She Said

conversationAudio.title: Level 2 - Lesson 3: He Said - She Said

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Today, Pete and I are meeting with a consultant who will help us with our new show. Yesterday, Pete had promised to meet me here at 8:00 am. but he did not come on time.

transcript.speaker: Prof Bot
transcript.text: Uh-oh. It’s bad to be late for a business meeting. But while we wait for Pete, let’s talk about a new verb tense -- past perfect! You know the past tense, right? Like, "Pete promised to meet me here at 8:00 a.m." Past perfect is a little different. When we talk about two things in the past, we can use the past perfect for the first event. Put "had" before the past participle. "Pete had promised he would meet Anna." Here's your assignment: find sentences with the past perfect tense. Remember, look for "had!"

transcript.speaker: Kelly
transcript.text: You two are late -- exactly 43 minutes late! What happened?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: He had to get his "special" coffee -- SPECIAL coffee!

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: She had to feed her birds -- HER birds!

transcript.speaker: Kelly
transcript.text: Okay, I can see already that you need my help. You can’t both talk at the same time. You have to take turns. Alright, Anna, you go first.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Sure. Kelly, see, Pete and I live in the same building. So, we decided to meet at 8:00 a.m. - 8:00 a.m. to come to work together. I had waited 15 minutes when Pete arrived!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: After Pete had wasted time waiting for coffee, we were late. I left you a message.*

transcript.speaker: Kelly
transcript.text: Hum. I didn’t get that message.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Oh. Sorry.

transcript.speaker: Kelly
transcript.text: Pete?

transcript.speaker: Prof. Bot
transcript.text: Anna left a message. That’s the right thing to do. Did you find some examples of the past perfect sentences? I did. Anna said,

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: "After Pete had wasted time waiting for coffee, we were late.
Look at that coffee! It looks more like dessert! Okay, keep watching for past perfect!

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: Yeah, that’s not why we’re late. This is why we’re late: I had arrived on time at 8:00 a.m. but didn’t see Anna. She was standing behind a tree. I think she was hugging it. I always walk to work. But she said that would take too long and that a scooter would be much faster. It was awful. I hated it. And it added too much time to our commute!
Then Anna stopped by a pond to feed the birds. She had named them after characters from books and yelled the names out loud … Romeo! Juliet! Sherlock!
By the time she had fed all the birds, we were late.

transcript.speaker: Kelly
transcript.text: This is what I think. You two see the same event very differently. Does this happen often with you two?

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Kelly
transcript.text: Okay. This is good. This is good! It’s good to see things differently. I have an idea: we will call the show "He Said, She Said." For every story, you tell a different point of view.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: That is a great idea, Kelly! Pete, we are different. That’s why I thought of you for this job!

transcript.speaker: Kelly
transcript.text: I think you two understand perfectly.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Let’s get to work!

transcript.speaker: Kelly
transcript.text: She named the birds? Really?

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: Yeah…
* Business people in the U.S. think you should come to a meeting at the exact time. If you are late to a business appointment, you should call and explain why.

items.title: Lesson 4: Run Away With the Circus!

mainVideo.title: Let’s Learn English - Level 2 - Lesson 4: Run Away With the Circus!

conversationAudio.title: Level 2 - Lesson 4: Let's Run Away With the Circus

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Hello, I’m Anna …

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: … and I’m Pete. Welcome to “He Said, Anna: … She Said”! Pete: Because there are always two sides … Anna: to every story! Anna: Today’s show is about Circus Arts! Pete: Circus? That’s not an art form. Anna: Yes, it is. Pete: No, it isn't. Anna: Yes, it is. Pete: No, it isn't. Anna: Yes, it is! Pete: No, it isn't. Anna: Yes, it is! Pete: No, it isn't. Anna: Yes, it is! Professor Bot: Oh dear. Anna and Pete do not agree about Circus Arts. But that's okay. Today’s lesson is about agreeing and disagreeing. Let’s listen to how Anna and Pete disagree or agree. Let’s hope these two can agree on something. Anna: Today, let’s run away with the circus! Recently, I went to a circus festival. There was a huge circus tent. And many different circus performers. It was a celebration of circus arts! Pete: That looks fun, Anna. But I don’t think circus performers are artists. I think they’re athletes with interesting skills … and costumes. Anna: Hmm, that is a very interesting point of view, Pete. And I completely disagree. Pete: Anna, Michelangelo was an artist. Rembrandt was an artist. People who swing from ropes are not artists. I know it’s not easy to swing from a bar and catch someone by the hands. You have to be very athletic to do that. Anna: That’s a good point, Pete. They are athletic. But they are called trapeze artists. Trapeze … ARTISTS. Pete: I hear what you’re saying, Anna. I do. But where is the art? Look at these guys. They’re jugglers. Anna: Yes, they are skilled in the art of juggling. Pete: They have a special skill. But are they artists? Anna: Yes! Pete: No! Pete: They're just throwing things back and forth. Anna: Kind of like you and me, Pete. We’re going back and forth on this issue. Pete: I don’t think we’ll ever agree on this one. Anna: No, but we can agree that these young people are amazing. Pete: Okay, yeah. We can agree on that. But, still, they are very athletic – flipping and throwing each other around. Anna: Yes, I agree with you on that point. Professor. Bot: They did it! They agreed!! Anna says she agrees that the performers are athletic. "That’s a good point, Pete. They are athletic. I agree with you on that point. " Now look for other ways they agree. Pete: Anna? Anna!! Anna: Sorry! Sorry! But he’s an artist too. He is telling a story with his sticks and his costume. Pete: What story? What costume? Anna: I see your point, Pete. I really do. But circus performers do more than physical tricks. Look! Look at these amazing performers! Pete: I will admit -- I like their costumes. Anna: You know, Pete. Let’s let the performers speak for themselves. Anna: Kate and Piper tell stories while hanging upside down on a ring! Pete: Was it hard to interview them upside down? Anna: I interviewed them right side up, Pete. Kate says circus performing may be athletic but it’s not competitive. With most sports, you compete. Kate: It’s an art form because like, other sports are competing. This is simply performing and having fun. Pete: Okay, Kate made a really good point. In athletics, there is a lot of competition. But still … Anna: Here’s Piper, Pete. Please pay attention, Pete. Pete: But, I - Anna: Shh. Piper: Well, when you’re up in the air doing circus you have to perform. And so, we learn to embody characters, and to move fluidly and gracefully … in artistic ways. Anna: And that …is why they are artists! Pete: You’re right, Anna. Oh, you’re right. It’s just so beautiful. Anna: I know. I know, Pete. Professor Bot: Good job you two! I'm so glad that Anna and Pete finally agree! Pete said, " You’re right, Anna." I agree, too. Circus arts are beautiful. Remember the website!

items.title: Lesson 5: Greatest Vacation of All Time

mainVideo.title: Let’s Learn English - Level 2 - Lesson 5: Greatest Vacation of All Time

conversationAudio.title: Level 2 - Lesson 5: The Greatest Vacation Ever!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: “Do you need a vacation?” Wow. That was the best vacation I have ever had … in my head. A beach is much better than here. I need a vacation!

transcript.speaker: Professor Bot
transcript.text: I hear you, Anna. I need a vacation too but not at the beach. Sand is not good for robots! When we compare things, we use special forms of adjectives. "Better" is a comparative adjective. That is used to compare two things. "Best" is a superlative adjective. It shows that one thing has more of ...something than ALL of the others. Try to find more of these adjectives. Look for ER or EST at the end.

transcript.speaker: Dan
transcript.text: NO! You can’t get your money back. I don’t care that it was your worst vacation ever!

transcript.speaker: Dan
transcript.text: Hello! Have a seat! Welcome to the World’s Best Vacation Travel Agency!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Thank you and congratulations!

transcript.speaker: Dan
transcript.text: For what?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: For being the world’s best travel agency.

transcript.speaker: Dan
transcript.text: Right … thanks.

transcript.speaker: Dan
transcript.text: Trudy, hold my calls. I am going to sell our most expensive vacation.

transcript.speaker: Trudy
transcript.text: Sure thing, Boss.

transcript.speaker: Dan
transcript.text: The Mountain Getaway is good for you. It’s a little pricey. But think of it -- you, on top of a mountain for seven days!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I’m afraid of high places.

transcript.speaker: Dan
transcript.text: Of course you are. That’s why our Deep Sea Adventure is better for you! It is pricier than the Mountain Getaway. Just you and the animals of the sea!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Shark! Shark!

transcript.speaker: Dan
transcript.text: No, there are no sharks in your dream vacation! You need the Safari Camp Out! It is our priciest vacation. But I think it’s the best one for you. During the day, you’ll see elephants, giraffes and lions. At night, you’ll sleep out under the stars.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Look, I think this was a bad idea.

transcript.speaker: Dan
transcript.text: Sure, you can leave. But then you won’t see the latest vacation technology.

transcript.speaker: Professor Bot
transcript.text: Did you find all of those adjectives? Dan started with good - The mountain getaway; then he moved to better - The Deep Sea Adventure. And finally, he said the Safari Campout was the best vacation for Anna!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Exactly what is the “latest vacation technology” … exactly?

transcript.speaker: Dan
transcript.text: I’m happy you asked. Meet the Travel Max 2000!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Wow.

transcript.speaker: Dan
transcript.text: So, tell me, how do you like to travel?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Well, I like travel that is cozy and romantic but still exciting.

transcript.speaker: Dan
transcript.text: Great. Tell me more.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I like traveling in a plane but not in a helicopter! Planes are a little scary but helicopters are scarier! My favorite way of traveling is by train. Ships can be the scariest! Have you seen the movie “Titanic”? Oh, and no horses. But I will ride a camel. And no bike tours. Biking is THE slowest AND least romantic way to travel. Excuse me, but I think the Travel Max 2000 is on fire.

transcript.speaker: Dan
transcript.text: Yes, we’re both on fire! We really want to sell you the most ex-, I mean, best vacation ever!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: No, I mean it’s really on fire!

transcript.speaker: Dan
transcript.text: You killed it. You killed the Travel Max 2000!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I am so sorry! Can I help you fix it?

transcript.speaker: Dan
transcript.text: No, no!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Don’t cry. I know what you need -- a vacation!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: The Safari Campout looks fun. It is the priciest. But I think you deserve it.

transcript.speaker: Dan
transcript.text: No, no!

transcript.speaker: Professor Bot
transcript.text: Oh Anna. This is the smokiest lesson yet! There were a lot of comparatives and superlatives but … I can’t breathe. Just go to the website to learn the best ways to use them!

mainVideo.title: Let’s Learn English - Level 2 - Lesson 6: Will It Float?

transcript.speaker: Penelope
transcript.text: Anna, thanks for taking me on a tour of D.C. today.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Sure thing, Penelope. You are new to town. And a tour is the best way to see more of the city!

transcript.speaker: Penelope
transcript.text: So, which tour are we taking – the one that goes through the city on a bus? Or the one that goes along the river in a boat?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Both!

transcript.speaker: Penelope
transcript.text: What? Anna, this isn’t going to be one of those trips, is it?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: No. Follow me.

transcript.speaker: Professor Bot
transcript.text: In this lesson, you are going to hear lots of prepositions! What’s a preposition, you ask? It’s a word that shows relationships between things. Anna says they are going on a tour through the city and along the river. Through and along are both prepositions. Watch for more!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Well, Penelope, there’s our ride!

transcript.speaker: Penelope
transcript.text: What is it?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: It’s the famous DC Ducks -- the boat with wheels! We will ride on the road and then sail on the water!

transcript.speaker: Penelope
transcript.text: Who thinks of these things?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I don't know. But I’m glad they do! Let’s get aboard, Sailor!

transcript.speaker: Penelope
transcript.text: (looking at a brochure about the boat) Hey, did you know that this bus … um, boat was created during World War II to carry people and supplies?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Wow. You know, a tour is so much more interesting with Fun Facts, like that one.

transcript.speaker: Penelope
transcript.text: I agree. I love Fun Facts!

transcript.speaker: Boy
transcript.text: Did I hear you say you love Fun Facts?
Anna & Penelope: Yeah.

transcript.speaker: Boy
transcript.text: Well, I have tons of Fun Facts for this tour!
Anna & Penelope: Great!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Penelope, where are his parents?

transcript.speaker: Penelope
transcript.text: Maybe - maybe he’s the Captain’s son and he helps his dad on tours!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Oh yeah! It would be so awesome to ride around the city in a boat all day with your dad!

transcript.speaker: Penelope
transcript.text: This is amazing, Anna. There are so many beautiful buildings along this road!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Hey, the Washington Monument is on the left!

transcript.speaker: Professor Bot
transcript.text: I have a Fun Fact too! Did you know that the Washington Monument was damaged in an earthquake? Whoa. Did you feel that?!

transcript.speaker: I heard
transcript.text: "around the city in a boat," "along this road and "on the left." All of these are prepositions showing place. Let's watch for more places and prepositions!

transcript.speaker: Penelope
transcript.text: Look, Anna, we’re across from the White House!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Penelope, the only thing between us and the President is the street … and a park … and a security gate .... and police officers … with guns.

transcript.speaker: Boy
transcript.text: Excuse me, do you want to know a Fun Fact about the White House?
Anna & Penelope: Yes!

transcript.speaker: Boy
transcript.text: Inside the White House there is a swimming pool, a movie theater and 32 bathrooms!

transcript.speaker: Penelope
transcript.text: Thirty-two bathrooms! That’s a lot of bathrooms!

transcript.speaker: Boy
transcript.text: I’d be happy with two. I live in a house with my mom, four sisters, two aunts and only one bathroom!

transcript.speaker: Penelope
transcript.text: Oh my! You know, Anna, we should give him a tip!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Of course! It is polite to tip your tour guide! Luckily, I have lots of dollar bills!

transcript.speaker: Penelope
transcript.text: That was a great Fun Fact! Here you go!

transcript.speaker: Boy
transcript.text: Thank you! I can tell you Fun Facts all day!

transcript.speaker: Professor Bot
transcript.text: Did you hear any more prepositions of place? I heard "between us and the president" “inside the White House" and "in a house."
And did you hear that the Duck Boat can go on the river? I don't believe it. Join us next time to find out which preposition we will use: The boat went ON the river or The boat went INTO the river?

conversationAudio.title: Level 2 - Lesson 7: Tip Your Tour Guide

transcript.speaker: Professor Bot
transcript.text: Welcome back! Anna and Penelope are taking a tour with DC Ducks. In this lesson, we are looking for prepositions. Listen for in, on, at, under and over - some important prepositions of place.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Penelope, the Lincoln Memorial is coming up on your left!

transcript.speaker: Boy
transcript.text: You’re going to love my Lincoln Memorial Fun Fact!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Oh, please tell us!

transcript.speaker: Boy
transcript.text: On a wall inside the memorial, the word “FUTURE” was carved wrong! They carved “EUTURE”!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Well, we all make mistakes.

transcript.speaker: Boy
transcript.text: Yeah, but this mistake was carved in stone!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: You’re right. That is pretty bad. Here’s another dollar!

transcript.speaker: Penelope
transcript.text: More fun facts, please! (Crossing the river) I love riding over bridges! The water looks so pretty from here!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Penelope, this is amazing! A minute ago, we were riding along the river, and now we’re riding in the river! Awesome.

transcript.speaker: Penelope
transcript.text: Hey, we’re passing by the Pentagon on our right!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Penelope, you love riding over the water on a bridge. But I love riding under a bridge in a boat!

transcript.speaker: Penelope
transcript.text: Anna, look! An airplane is flying right over our heads!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Wow! This is the closest I’ve ever been to an airplane in flight. Well, I’ve been inside a flying airplane. But not outside of an airplane as it flies over my head!

transcript.speaker: Penelope
transcript.text: And now we’re driving out of the water. I still can’t believe this thing drives and sails!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I know. It’s amazing.

transcript.speaker: Boy
transcript.text: After we ride along these railroad tracks, you’ll see my favorite part of the tour! The U.S. Treasury where they make money!

transcript.speaker: Professor Bot
transcript.text: That young man is making a lot of money, too. Did you hear these prepositions? On your left, on our right, in the river, over bridges, over our heads, over my head, on a bridge. As you watch more, look for 'inside' and 'outside.'

transcript.speaker: Penelope
transcript.text: Look, the U.S. Capitol is coming up!

transcript.speaker: Boy
transcript.text: I have a great Fun Fact about the U.S. Capitol.

transcript.speaker: Penelope
transcript.text: What is it?

transcript.speaker: Boy
transcript.text: There are tunnels under the Capitol. They connect the Capitol and office buildings of lawmakers.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I bet they built them years ago for secret reasons!

transcript.speaker: Boy
transcript.text: No. The lawmakers did not want to walk around outside in bad weather.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Oh.

transcript.speaker: Penelope
transcript.text: We’re back at Union Station!

transcript.speaker: Boy
transcript.text: Do you want to know a creepy Fun Fact about Union Station? (he points to Union Station)

transcript.speaker: Penelope
transcript.text: The creepier the better!

transcript.speaker: Boy
transcript.text: Many years ago, inside Union Station, there was a funeral home!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: A funeral home?! You mean, for dead people?!

transcript.speaker: Boy
transcript.text: Do you know another kind of funeral home?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: No!

transcript.speaker: Boy
transcript.text: Well, I’ve gotta run!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Thanks for giving us the great tour!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Captain, that was awesome! And your son is a great tour guide!

transcript.speaker: Captain
transcript.text: What son?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Him.

transcript.speaker: Captain
transcript.text: I’ve never seen that boy in my life! See ya, ladies!

transcript.speaker: Professor Bot
transcript.text: I learned many new Fun Facts in this lesson. Did you learn about prepositions?
Here’s a list of all the prepositions used in this lesson. Wow! That’s a lot! I know, let’s not read them. Let’s sing them! Hit it, boys! Take it away singers!
since at through aboard behind to about by near across for of ahead from on around in until over like with

transcript.speaker: Anna

transcript.speaker: Kelly
transcript.text: Sure.

transcript.speaker: Anna

transcript.speaker: Prof. Bot
transcript.text: Hi English learners! Your lesson today is about my favorite food -- barbecue! Your assignment is to find passive sentences. What are those, you might ask? In passive sentences the subject receives the action!
For example, “Anna was sent to cover a food festival.”
Passive sentences have a form of the BE verb + the past participle of the main verb. This lesson is LOADED with passive sentences. Hey! That’s a passive sentence, too!
Okay, now, it’s Barbecue Time!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Today, a Barbecue Battle is being held in Washington, D.C. This festival, which is known as one of the biggest food festivals in the United States, brings together barbecue lovers from all over the country! Barbecue is meat that is cooked over an open fire or on a grill.

Chicken, pork and beef are all common meats to grill on a barbecue! No matter which meat you like to barbecue, the sauce is very important. Sauces are taken very seriously by chefs. Most ingredients are kept secret!
So, can you tell us what is in your barbecue sauce?
Chef 1: No, I can’t tell you.

transcript.speaker: Anna

transcript.speaker: Anna

transcript.speaker: Prof. Bot

Professor Bot loves Barbecue!
Barbecue is loved by Prof. Bot.
Good job! And yes, I do.

transcript.speaker: Anna

The states of Texas, North and South Carolina and the cities of Memphis and Kansas City are known as the Barbecue Belt. People who are loyal to barbecue are really loyal to their favorite barbecue. Person 3: Kansas City!
Person 4: Memphis style!
Person 3: Kansas City!
Person 5: Texas!
Person 3: Kansas!
Person 5: Texas!
Person 3: Kansas!
Person 5: Texas!
Person 3: I say Kansas.
Person 5: Texas!

transcript.speaker: Anna

transcript.speaker: Bruna
transcript.text: Hi, Anna!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Hi, Bruna! What’s up?

transcript.speaker: Bruna
transcript.text: I thought we could meet for lunch today.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I wish I could, but I can’t. I have to research Peru for a story.

transcript.speaker: Bruna
transcript.text: How’s it going?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Not so good. I’ve been reading about Peru and listening to Peruvian music. I really want to understand Peru. I hope it's enough.

transcript.speaker: Bruna

transcript.speaker: Anna

transcript.speaker: Bruna

transcript.speaker: Bruna
transcript.text: No, I don’t mean to really go there. The museum where I work is having a Peruvian festival today! …. Anna? Anna? Anna, are you there?

transcript.speaker: Prof. Bot
transcript.text: Hello again! Professor Bot here. Today we will hear about wishes and hopes. Bruna asked Anna to go to lunch, but she answered,
I wish I could, but I can’t. Listen for more hope and wish sentences.

transcript.speaker: Bruna
transcript.text: Hi, Anna!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Hi, Bruna! Thanks for telling me about this event.

transcript.speaker: Bruna
transcript.text: Sure! It's much better than staring at your computer. I hope it helps with your story.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I’m sure it will. So, what should we see first?

transcript.speaker: Bruna
transcript.text: Dance and music are very important to Peruvian culture, so let’s watch the dancers.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Great! Let’s go!

transcript.speaker: Bruna
transcript.text: There's this very special Peruvian dance called Marinera Norteña.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I love the Marinera Nortina… !

transcript.speaker: Bruna
transcript.text: Marinera Norteña.

transcript.speaker: Anna

transcript.speaker: Bruna
transcript.text: No. Marinera Norteña.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I love the … marriage dance!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Bruna, I read about this dance. But it is much more romantic in person!

transcript.speaker: Bruna
transcript.text: The dancers are giving lessons after their performance. You should try it!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I’d love to. But I’m not ready to get married. I mean, one day I hope to meet the right guy. We’ll buy matching motorcycles and ride into the sunset -- the wind blowing through our hair!

transcript.speaker: Bruna
transcript.text: Anna, the dance just shows the courtship tradition. It doesn’t mean you will get married.

transcript.speaker: Anna

transcript.speaker: Bruna

transcript.speaker: Anna

transcript.speaker: Bruna

transcript.speaker: Anna

transcript.text: Great. See you then!

transcript.speaker: Bruna

transcript.text: Did you notice any sentences with hope or wish?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Oh, wow! I can make my own Peruvian art!

transcript.speaker: Bruna

transcript.speaker: Anna

transcript.speaker: Bruna

transcript.speaker: Bruna

transcript.speaker: Bruna

transcript.speaker: Anna

mainVideo.title: Let’s Learn English - Level 2 - Lesson 11: The Big Snow

transcript.speaker: Kelly
transcript.text: Hi, Anna. Why do you have all this weather stuff?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I love weather.

transcript.speaker: Kelly
transcript.text: Me too! Weather is so important.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: It is. It affects people’s lives!

transcript.speaker: Kelly
transcript.text: Have you ever reported on a big weather event?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I have. I’ve reported on a blizzard.

transcript.speaker: Kelly
transcript.text: Do mean the one last weekend?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Yes! I had been waiting for that blizzard for years. When it came, I was ready.

transcript.speaker: Prof. Bot
transcript.text: Welcome to our most perfect lesson! Why is it perfect? Today we are reviewing the present perfect and past perfect verb tenses. These show that an action is completed.
Kelly uses the present perfect when she says,

transcript.speaker: Kelly
transcript.text: Have you ever reported on a big weather event?
Anna uses the past perfect when she says,

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I had been waiting for that blizzard for years.
Listen for "have" or "had" and the past participle to find more sentences with the perfect tense. I'll color those words to help you.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I have wanted to report on a big weather event my whole life.

transcript.speaker: Kelly
transcript.text: Who hasn’t? Did you report all weekend ... by yourself?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: No, no. I volunteered Pete to help me.

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: Why am I here on a Saturday? Why are you carrying things? Why? Why?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Pete, these are my supplies – food, a blanket; warm clothing. Where are your supplies?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Pete, Pete, Pete. This could be the “blizzard of the century.”

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: It’ll be fine.

transcript.speaker: Kelly
transcript.text: How else had you prepared?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Well, I had just bought the latest weather forecasting software. So, I brought it!

transcript.speaker: Kelly
transcript.text: Do you mean The Weather Genie Pro?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: You know it. Pete thought it was pretty great too.

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: Do you have any games on that thing?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Yes! I have the best weather survival game. Boom!

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: Sounds fun.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: It is. But right now, Pete, this computer is a work tool. It will give us the temperature, wind speed, wind direction and amount of snowfall … in real time! Boom, boom!

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: I can’t wait.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Pete, we need a name for this blizzard.

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: No, we don’t.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: All the great storms have names.

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: No, they don’t.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I know -- “The Big Snow!”

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: I am not saying “The Big Snow.”

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: Welcome to “The Big Snow.”

transcript.speaker: Kelly
transcript.text: The Big Snow broke all kinds of records, didn’t it?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Yes it did. And every time a record was broken, we celebrated!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: So far, in Washington, D.C. 29 inches of snow has fallen. That, my dear listeners, is a record! (Honks horn)

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: We just broke the wind speed record! (Honks horn)

transcript.speaker: Anna

transcript.text: By Saturday night, stores and restaurants had closed. Did you bring enough food?

transcript.speaker: Anna

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Hey, Pete, where is my bag of popcorn?

transcript.text: Maybe you ate it already.

transcript.speaker: Anna

transcript.speaker: Anna

transcript.text: Wow. That must have been a great team-building exercise for you and Pete.

transcript.speaker: Anna

mainVideo.title: Let’s Learn English - Level 2 - Lesson 12: Run! Bees!

transcript.text: (blue text shows conditional sentences)

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Wow. Did you know that bees are dying?

transcript.speaker: Kaveh
transcript.text: That is bad news. If all the bees died, there would be no food. Bees are very important.
(buzz sound)

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Yes, they are. Speaking of bees, one of our little friends is here now.

transcript.speaker: Kaveh
transcript.text: You know, Anna, if you ignore it, it will fly away. But if you swat it, it might sting you.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I’ll ignore it. I can ignore it. See, I’m ignoring it. (she is swatting at the bee)

transcript.speaker: Kaveh
transcript.text: Anna, are you afraid of bees?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: What makes you say that?

transcript.speaker: Kaveh
transcript.text: Anna, you should call my friend, Caroline. She is a beekeeper and a bee educator. If you talk to her, she’ll probably help you get over your fear of bees.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I am not afraid of bees.

transcript.speaker: Kaveh
transcript.text: Here’s her card.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Ahhh!

transcript.speaker: Prof. Bot
transcript.text: In this lesson, you can learn about conditionals. They have "if" and "will" or "would." There are two kinds of conditional sentences in this lesson.
Type 1 conditionals have a real event, and a result that probably will happen. Chances are good. Here is the pattern:
If +present tense verb ... will + future tense verb.

transcript.speaker: Kaveh uses this when he says
transcript.text: "If you ignore it, it will fly away."
Type 2 conditionals have a possible event and a result that may or may not happen. We don't know. Here is the pattern:
If + past tense verb ...would + infinitive verb.
Kaveh uses this pattern when he says, "If all the bees died, there would be no food."
Look for the "if" in a sentence to find more conditionals in today's lesson. I'll color them, too!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I think I'm at the wrong address. This does not look like a place where bees are kept. ​(knocks on door)

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Oh, sorry to bother you. I’m looking for beekeeper Caroline. I’m here to take her “Learn to Love Bees!” class.

transcript.speaker: Caroline
transcript.text: You’re in the right place! I’m Caroline!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Oh, nice to meet you! Um, Caroline, I thought this class used real bees and real hives.

transcript.speaker: Caroline
transcript.text: It does! If you look in my backyard, you will see my bees! I’m a home beekeeper!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: What? You live with bees? That is really amazing! And at the same time really scary.

transcript.speaker: Caroline
transcript.text: It’s not scary. If you come, I’ll show you.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Caroline, how many bees are in that hive?

transcript.speaker: Caroline
transcript.text: About thirty thousand (30,000) in each.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: What? That's amazing! But, aren’t you afraid that they are gonna come out and kill you?

transcript.speaker: Caroline
transcript.text: No, not at all, Anna. Even my children help me. Tell me, why are you afraid of bees?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I don't know. Well, when I was a little girl my mom ran out of honey. And I really wanted honey for my pancakes. So, I climbed high into a tree and hit a beehive with a stick … several times. Then I reached inside with my bare hands to pull the honey out. That’s when I got stung … a lot.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Caroline, if you hit a beehive with a stick and reach inside, you might get stung.

transcript.speaker: Caroline
transcript.text: No, Anna. If you do those things, you will get stung.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Yes. I did.

transcript.speaker: Caroline
transcript.text: And you know that it was your fault you got stung, don’t you?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Yes. I did.

transcript.speaker: Caroline
transcript.text: Bees know your feelings. And if you stay calm, the bees will be calm. If you're nervous, the bees will be nervous. And if bees are nervous, they may sting. So, please be calm.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I will be calm. I am calm. Okay, I'm ready. I'm ready

transcript.speaker: Caroline
transcript.text: Great. Let’s get our equipment on.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Wait! Wait! I’m not ready! I'm nervous! Give me a minute to be calm.

transcript.speaker: Prof. Bot
transcript.text: Are you ready for one more conditional sentence?
If you are not afraid, you will join us next time to learn more about bees!

mainVideo.title: Let’s Learn English - Level 2 - Lesson 13: Save the Bees!

transcript.text: (blue font shows conditional sentences)

transcript.speaker: Prof. Bot
transcript.text: We are back with Anna and Caroline and the bees. Last time, Anna was afraid. (Anna: I'm not afraid of bees!) But Caroline is helping her to stay safe. Look at sentences that start with "If" to find more conditional sentences. Remember, Type 1 conditionals use the present tense and "will," and Type 2 use the past tense and "would." Now, let's find out what happens with Anna and the bees.

transcript.speaker: Caroline
transcript.text: I have a feeling that your fear of bees will be gone soon. There are things beekeepers do to protect ourselves. For example, we wear protective clothing. This is a beekeeper’s veil, suit and gloves. There are other things we can do, too. If I use a smoker, the bees will stay calm.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Let’s use smoke … lots of smoke.

transcript.speaker: Caroline
transcript.text: Okay, Anna, that’s enough smoke. Another thing you can do is stay calm. Okay. When I lift the frame, you will see the bees.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I’m ready. Let's do this thing!

transcript.speaker: Caroline
transcript.text: Okay, let's put on our protective clothing.

transcript.speaker: Caroline
transcript.text: I will carefully take out a frame. This is where the bees live. There are worker bees, drone bees and the queen bee. The bees have different jobs. The queen bee lays the eggs. The worker bees collect nectar and pollen ​from flowers and bring it back to the hive. Then they make honey! Now, you hold the frame. There are the bees.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: There are so many! And they are so busy! Now I know why we say, “busy as a bee!”

transcript.speaker: Caroline
transcript.text: Good job, Anna.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Caroline, bees are beautiful and important. If I wanted to help the bees, what would I do?

transcript.speaker: Caroline
transcript.text: Great question. You can plant native flowers that bees like. Here’s a book to help you know which ones to plant.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: It’s a beautiful book. And look, it tells you which bees like which types of flowers.

transcript.speaker: Caroline
transcript.text: It also tells you how the flowers affect the flavor of the honey.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Flowers make a big difference to bees. If they don’t eat, they won’t live.

transcript.speaker: Caroline
transcript.text: Buying local honey also helps the bees. If you want to help bees, do those two things.

transcript.speaker: Prof Bot
transcript.text: I learned a lot about bees. Hey, if I worked with bees, I would not need protective clothing! Guess what? That was a Type 2 conditional. And I heard a Type 1 conditional, too. (Anna: If they don’t eat, they won’t live.)

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Thanks for the book, Caroline, and the bee puppet and for teaching me about bees. Look … I’m not scared.

transcript.speaker: Caroline
transcript.text: Good job, Anna. If you ever want to see the bees again, I’ll be here! You have my business card. I'll let you see yourself out.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Thanks! Bye! I will plant tons of flowers!

transcript.speaker: Bees
transcript.text: Thanks, Anna. (bees spell out the words)

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Sure thing, bees! Oh, and I'm sorry about hitting that hive when I was a little girl.

transcript.speaker: Bees
transcript.text: We love you, Anna. (bees make a heart sign.)

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Take care, bees! (to herself) Which way is the Metro?

transcript.speaker: Bees
transcript.text: That way. (they draw an arrow)

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Thanks!

transcript.speaker: Prof. Bot
transcript.text: So, if I you want to learn more about bees, visit your local beekeeper like Anna did. Maybe you can try some local honey, too.
Now it’s your turn. Practice making conditional sentences. If you practice, you will become better at them. That's type 1!

transcript.text: Hello! What are you guys looking at?

They are also using adverb clauses.
Adverb clauses tell us when, why, how, where and under what conditions.

transcript.speaker: Kaveh

transcript.speaker: Professor Bot

Used to and would describe something that happened repeatedly in the past.
Kaveh uses would when he says, “When I first started working here, I would go every day!
There are two differences between used to and would.
Number 1: We use would only when we say the time period first.
Number 2: For verbs like be, think, feel, see and understand, we can only use used to.
Kaveh says, "It used to be across from the cafeteria."
Keep listening for more!

mainVideo.title: Let’s Learn English - Level 2 - Lesson 17: Flour Baby, Part 1

transcript.speaker: Ms. Weaver
transcript.text: Anna, Pete, I have a new assignment for you -- a show on single parents! What is it like for a mother or a father to raise a child by herself or himself?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: We can interview single parents. They can share their experiences themselves.

transcript.speaker: Ms. Weaver
transcript.text: Yes, but you need to experience parenthood yourselves.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Ourselves?

transcript.speaker: Peter
transcript.text: Yeah, how do we do that? We’re not parents.

transcript.speaker: Ms. Weaver
transcript.text: I asked myself the same question. I said, "Caty, how are they gonna do that?" Then an idea came to me. I will give you the babies!

transcript.speaker: Professor Bot
transcript.text: You may be asking yourself the same thing that I’m asking myself: what is Ms. Weaver talking about!? I am sure we will find out shortly.
This lesson teaches reflexive pronouns.
Reflexive pronouns refer back to the subject of a sentence or clause. We use them when the subject and the object are the same person or thing.
For example, Ms. Weaver says, “I asked myself the same question.”
“I” is the subject and “myself” refers back to it. Here, she would not use the pronoun “me.” You need to use the reflexive pronoun “myself.”

transcript.speaker: Reflexive pronouns are easy to find
transcript.text: they end in “self” or “selves.” I have a feeling we are going to see a lot of reflexive pronouns. Listen for them!
(Pete and Anna continue their meeting with Ms. Weaver. She puts two bags of flour on the table. Pete and Anna still look confused.)

transcript.speaker: Ms. Weaver
transcript.text: Here are your babies!

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: Those are bags of flour.

transcript.speaker: Ms. Weaver
transcript.text: No, Pete, for the next six days, this is your baby. Here are your instructions. Do not leave your babies alone. A baby cannot take care of itself. And you two must do everything by yourselves.
We will meet next Friday. Oh, and the person who does the best research will get an extra day of vacation. Help yourself to a baby.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Pete, look, my baby is organic and whole grain. Your baby is ordinary.
(Pete pushes her flour baby off desk.)

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: (to Pete) Monster! (to Caty) This is a great idea, Ms. Weaver!
(Pete and Anna are now outside.)

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: This is a terrible idea.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Speak for yourself, Pete! We need to throw ourselves into the research! I’m starting right now!
(She leaves but forgets her Flour Baby.)

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: Hey Anna, you forgot your baby!
(She turns and looks at Pete.)

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Come to mama!
(The bag of flour flies at her. She catches it.)

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Good girl! Good girl!

transcript.speaker: Professor Bot
transcript.text: Singular reflexive pronouns end in “self.” Plural ones end in “selves.”
Anna says, “We need to throw ourselves into the research!” The subject “we” is plural. So, we must use the plural reflexive pronoun “ourselves.”

(The parenting research begins. Anna tries to open a baby stroller but can’t. A man walking by helps her. She pushes Flour Baby in the stroller but it falls out. On another day, she jogs with it. After several days, she is tired!)

transcript.speaker: Professor Bot
transcript.text: We will all see how Pete is doing in the next episode. We’ll also learn when not to use reflexive pronouns.

mainVideo.title: Let’s Learn English - Level 2 - Lesson 18: Flour Baby, Part 2

transcript.speaker: Professor Bot
transcript.text: In Part 1 of this two-part lesson, Ms. Weaver gave Anna and Pete an assignment. Ms. Weaver instructed them to do everything by themselves.
“Themselves” is a reflexive pronoun.
In today’s lesson, Ms. Weaver will look at Pete’s and Anna’s research. First, let’s see Pete’s experiment.
(Pete throws the bag of flour on his chair and throws many other things on his flour baby. Next, we see him outside enjoying ice-cream without his flour baby.)

transcript.speaker: Ms. Weaver
transcript.text: Okay, Pete, let me see your research first.
(Pete hands her a big binder filled with research.)

transcript.speaker: Ms. Weaver
transcript.text: That’s a heavy binder. And you and your Baby look great.

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: Thanks, Ms. Weaver. We feel great!

transcript.speaker: Ms. Weaver
transcript.text: Anna. Anna, you’re next. Anna? Anna wake up!
(She wakes up but is very confused.)

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I'm here, Baby! I’m here! I’m here! Here's your bottle.
(She accidentally squirts her bottle and milk goes everywhere.)

transcript.speaker: Ms. Weaver
transcript.text: Anna, you and your baby look awful. What happened?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Well, I took her everywhere. Everywhere. And I fed her every three hours. So, I haven’t slept since … what day is it?

transcript.speaker: Ms. Weaver
transcript.text: It’s Friday. What happened there?
(Ms. Weaver points to a large bandage on Anna’s flour baby.)

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Oh, that. Oh, that. I was making myself a salad and had a little accident with a knife. I put my flour baby in front of me. And then I accidentally stabbed it. But I gave it First Aid!

transcript.speaker: Ms. Weaver
transcript.text: Is that a burn?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Yes. Yes it is. While I was making myself dinner, I put Baby next to me. I accidentally knocked her into the sink. So I put her in the microwave to dry. That’s when she caught fire.
(Pete smiles, thinking he’s won.)

transcript.speaker: Professor Bot
transcript.text: Okay. So, we use a reflexive pronoun when it refers to the subject of a sentence or clause.
But we DON’T use a reflexive pronoun with prepositions of place.

transcript.speaker: Anna uses examples of both in one sentence
transcript.text: While I was making myself dinner, I put Baby next to me.
We use a reflexive pronoun in the first part of the sentence. “Myself” refers to the subject “I.”
But in the second part of the sentence, we don’t use a reflexive pronoun in the prepositional phrase. We use the pronoun “me.” Why? “next to” is a preposition of place.
(Back in the meeting room, we’re about to learn who won the parenting experiment. Pete is smiling, thinking he won.)

transcript.speaker: Ms. Weaver
transcript.text: Anna, Anna, you should be very proud of yourself.

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: Proud? She stabbed and burned her baby!! And she only did one page of research…and it’s covered in milk. Ew.

transcript.speaker: Ms. Weaver
transcript.text: Yes, Pete. But she followed instructions.

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: Hey, I did ...

transcript.speaker: Ms. Weaver
transcript.text: Please, Pete. Anna, I think your baby has lost some weight. Is there something else you want to share?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Yes. I’d like to share … these! I made them myself this morning.

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: You baked your baby? You should be ashamed of yourself!

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: I baked them at the end of the experiment, Pete. At that point, this was just a bag of flour.

transcript.speaker: Pete

transcript.speaker: Ms. Weaver

transcript.speaker: Pete

transcript.speaker: Pete

transcript.speaker: Professor Bot
transcript.text: So, what have we learned? We’ve learned when to use reflexive pronouns and when not to.

transcript.text: Anna, Penelope and Rick are making a news story about the Washington Car Show. Ms. Weaver gave them instructions.

There are two ways to do this. One is to use the person’s exact words and use quotation marks. We call this "direct speech."
For example, Ms. Weaver had said, “You need to show lots of cars.”
The other way is to talk about what someone said. We call this "reported speech."

transcript.speaker: Anna tells Penelope
transcript.text: She said that we need to show lots of cars.
In this sentence, "she," is the subject, “said” is the reporting verb, “that” is the conjunction and “we need to show lots of cars” is the reporting clause.
Keep watching, and listen for sentences where Anna talks about what someone else said!

transcript.speaker: Professor Bot
transcript.text: Did you hear Ashley and Anna using the words talk and speak?
Talk and speak both mean “to say words.” And, many times, you can use either word without losing any meaning. But there are some differences in when we use these words.
The word talk is usually used:
for conversations between two or more people and informal situations, such as between friends or family
For example, Ashley asks Anna: “Are you talking to yourself again?”
Speak is usually used:
for one-way communication, such as presentations formal situations, such as a boss speaking with her workers to talk about language ability and in polite requests
Keep watching, and listen for the words talk and speak.

transcript.speaker: Sue
transcript.text: Welcome to class, Anna. I can’t wait to see your trash!

transcript.speaker: Sue

transcript.speaker: Anna

transcript.speaker: Sue
transcript.text: Okay. So...it’s a plastic helmet.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: This plastic helmet said, “Anna. Hey, Anna, find me a head.”

transcript.speaker: Sue
transcript.text: Okay, um...and a broken toy.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: This broken toy … this broken toy said to me – it said, “Anna, help me find fun.” “Help me, Anna” is what it said.

transcript.speaker: Sue
transcript.text: Anna, this stuff is not saying anything to you or me or anyone. It’s what we like to call in the business … garbage.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: But you said to bring in trash.

transcript.speaker: Sue
transcript.text: Sometimes trash is treasure. Sometimes it's just trash.

transcript.speaker: Sue
transcript.text: Anna, don’t worry. Next week, I could teach you decoupage.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Decoupage. Decoupage. That’s fun to say.

transcript.speaker: Sue

transcript.speaker: Anna

transcript.speaker: Prof. Bot
transcript.text: Ut oh. It looks like Anna doesn’t know the difference between treasure and trash. She thinks those things are telling her something!

transcript.speaker: Prof. Bot
transcript.text: The words tell and say have similar meanings. But we use them in different ways.

transcript.speaker: Prof Bot
transcript.text: Tell means “to inform or instruct someone with words” and is almost always followed by an indirect object. For example, Sue says, “Tell me about that.”

transcript.speaker: Prof. Bot
transcript.text: The word me is the indirect object and tells us who is being told.

transcript.speaker: Prof. Bot
transcript.text: Say means “to express something with words” and focuses more on the words used. For example, Anna says, “That’s what it said. It said, ‘Use me, Anna.’”

transcript.speaker: Prof. Bot
transcript.text: Listen for when Anna and Sue use tell and say.

transcript.speaker: Anna

transcript.speaker: Sue

transcript.speaker: Anna

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Hi! I see you like superhero culture. Me too.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: In fact, tonight I’m going to the big superhero convention. Are you going?

transcript.speaker: YOUNG MAN
transcript.text: Um, I don’t know.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Well, you'd better decide soon. Last year, it sold out.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: So, since we’re talking about superheroes: would you rather become a superhero by accident, like Spiderman, or be born a superhero, like Wonder Woman?

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Take your time. It’s a big question. I thought about it for days –

transcript.speaker: YOUNG MAN
transcript.text: Okay. If I had to choose, I’d rather be born a superhero.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: I’d rather become a superhero by an unexpected accident!

transcript.speaker: YOUNG MAN
transcript.text: Aren’t all accidents unexpected?

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Well, yeah.

transcript.speaker: YOUNG MAN
transcript.text: What was that!? Are you okay?

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: I'm better than okay. I feel super!

transcript.speaker: PROF. BOT
transcript.text: Oh No! Anna was just hit by lightning. She had better get help.

transcript.speaker: PROF. BOT
transcript.text: We use had better to give advice. It is very informal and stronger than should and ought to. For example, Anna says: “You'd better decide soon. Last year, it sold out.”

transcript.speaker: PROF. BOT
transcript.text: When we use had better, we usually shorten the word had for personal pronouns.

transcript.speaker: PROF. BOT
transcript.text: We use would rather to say what we or someone else prefers to do or have. For example, the boy says: “Okay. If I had to choose, I’d rather be born a superhero.

transcript.speaker: PROF. BOT
transcript.text: With would rather, we also shorten the word would when used with personal pronouns. Keep watching and listen for had better and would rather.

transcript.speaker: YOUNG MAN
transcript.text: You’d better see a doctor.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: I’ve never felt better!

transcript.speaker: YOUNG MAN
transcript.text: You were just struck by lightning!! And what happened to your hair and your clothes?

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: I don't know. Wait, I do know. This is my super suit! And this is my origin story.

transcript.speaker: YOUNG MAN
transcript.text: What are you talking about?

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: An origin story tells the beginning of a superhero. You should know that.

transcript.speaker: YOUNG MAN
transcript.text: You're not making any sense, lady.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: I would rather be called Lightning Bolt Lady! It’ll sound great in a theme song: Lightning Bolt Lady!

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Now, I need to find my superpowers --

transcript.speaker: YOUNG MAN
transcript.text: Um, I really think --

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Wait. Don’t tell me. I’ll read your mind. You are thinking you’d like to be my super helper.

transcript.speaker: YOUNG MAN
transcript.text: I was not thinking that.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: ... that you’d like to live in a treehouse.

transcript.speaker: YOUNG MAN
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: … that you should eat more vegetables.

transcript.speaker: YOUNG MAN
transcript.text: Please, stop talking. You really should get some help.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Mind reading is not my superpower. Maybe I can become invisible. I … am … invisible!

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: You can’t see me. Who am I? I’m not here. You can’t see me.

transcript.speaker: YOUNG MAN
transcript.text: I can see you and so can everybody else.

transcript.speaker: ANNA

transcript.speaker: ANNA

mainVideo.title: Let’s Learn English - Level 2 - Lesson 26: Look-alikes

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: This article is so interesting. Pete, listen to this: “Somewhere in the world there is someone who looks just like you.” Pete: No one is this handsome. Anna: Oh Pete, there’s something between your teeth. (Pete tries to clean his teeth.) Pete: It is gone? Anna: No. No. It’s still there. There. You got it. But think of it: There could be two of us in the world! Pete: Two Annas? Pete: Actually, Anna, maybe your silly article is right. Yesterday at work, I met a woman who looks just like you. Anna: Really? Wait, are you making fun of me? Pete: Not this time. Pete: She’s tall and has curly hair. But even her face looks like yours. I think she’s a career consultant. Anna: I bet she has a lot of great advice. I can’t wait to meet her. Pete: Yes, you can. I met her and she is very difficult. Anna: Pete, she’s just new. We have to give her a chance. What’s her name? Pete: Evelyna or something like that. You can’t miss her. She always wears a hat. Penelope: So, Anna, have you met the new consultant yet? Anna: No. But I’ve already heard. We look alike, don’t we? Penelope: Yeah, but you don’t act alike. You’re much nicer than she is. Anna: Maybe she gets nervous at new jobs. Or maybe she’s shy. Let’s not judge, Penelope. Penelope: She’s not nervous or shy. She’s mean. Anna: You know, we should get to know her better. Let’s invite her to lunch! Penelope: Sorry but I’m busy that day. (Penelope walks away. Anna yells after her.) Anna: Oh, that’s too bad. Hey, I haven’t picked a day yet! (Anna and Pete are playing a game.) Anna: This is going to be so much fun. Boy, I can’t wait to play this game. Evilana: How much longer are you going to be? Anna: We’ll be just a minute … (Anna turns around and sees her look-alike.) Anna: You must be Evelana. I’m Anna. We are look-alikes! Evilana: No, we’re not. And my name is pronounced “Evil-ana.” Pete: Oh. This is going to be fun. Evilana: You had better hurry up. I need this room for a lecture. It’s called: “If You Want to Win, Others Must Lose.” What is all this stuff, anyway? Anna: It’s a game. We’re going to play at lunch. Evilana: It’s a stupid child’s game! Anna: It’s a fun game. But yes, it is for children. Evilana: Well, you may be childish but I’m not. And you look stupid with that thing on your head. Anna: Well, you look serious with that look on your face. Come on, Pete. Let’s play somewhere else. Pete: Actually, I’m going to stay for Evilana’s lecture. Anna: Fine. You can learn new ways to beat people. Evilana: He will. He will. (Days later, Anna and Penelope are playing the game. Pete comes in. He has a problem with his eye.) Anna: Okay. Am I a food? Penelope: Nope. Pete: Hey, do you guys have room for one more? Penelope: Sure, Pete! Come on over. What happened to your eye? Pete: Evilana “accidentally” hit me. And she didn’t even say sorry. She’s so mean! Penelope: I told you so. Anna: Here, Pete. Put on this headband. You’ll feel better. Penelope, you’re right. Evilana is an awful person! Penelope: And violent. And now we have to work with her! Anna: Haven’t you heard? She’s gone! She was given another assignment. Penelope: What assignment? Anna: I’m not sure. I think it has something to do with outdoors. Anyway, let’s play! Pete it’s your turn.
Evilana is the new career consultant at The Studio. But how long will she stay?

mainVideo.title: Let’s Learn English - Level 2 - Lesson 27: Fish out of Water

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Hello, Ms. Weaver!

transcript.speaker: MS. WEAVER
transcript.text: Oh, Anna. I’ve invited some people to dinner Saturday. We’re going to that new seafood restaurant -- Fish on a Dish.

transcript.speaker: MS. WEAVER
transcript.text: Why don’t you join us? My treat.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Thanks, Ms. Weaver. But I already have plans. My friend has invited me to her houseboat.

transcript.speaker: MS. WEAVER
transcript.text: Houseboat, really? That’s unique.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Yes, it is. In fact, I’m thinking of living on a houseboat.

transcript.speaker: MS. WEAVER
transcript.text: Aren’t you too tall and klutzy to live on a houseboat?

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: I am not too tall!
(She knocks over a display board.)

transcript.speaker: PROF. BOT VO
transcript.text: Is Anna really ready for a houseboat?

transcript.speaker: PROF. BOT
transcript.text: Ms. Weaver invited Anna to dinner. When we make friendly, informal invitations, we use phrases like “Why don’t…?”

transcript.speaker: PROF. BOT
transcript.text: For example, Ms. Weaver said, “Why don’t you join us? My treat!” That’s: Why don’t plus the subject plus the simple form of the verb.

transcript.speaker: PROF. BOT
transcript.text: Anna responded to the invitation by saying, “Thanks, but I already have plans.” Keep watching for more examples of informal invitations!

transcript.speaker: FANNY
transcript.text: Anna, I’m so glad you could come!

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Hi, Fanny!

transcript.speaker: FANNY
transcript.text: Hi, this is my son, Phoenix.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Hi, Phoenix.

transcript.speaker: FANNY
transcript.text: How about you give Anna a tour and I will make some lunch?

transcript.speaker: PHOENIX
transcript.text: Aye, aye, captain!

transcript.speaker: FANNY
transcript.text: Great!

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Do you really call her “captain”?

transcript.speaker: PHOENIX

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: So, Phoenix, I think I’d like to live on a houseboat. Do you like living here?

transcript.speaker: PHOENIX
transcript.text: I love it! It’s much different than living in a house.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Oh, I bet. I bet you had to get rid of a lot of stuff, didn’t you?

transcript.speaker: PHOENIX
transcript.text: No way! We moved from a 3-story house to a boat! So, we really had to downsize!

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: I’d have to get rid of a lot of stuff. I have a rock collection and I have some really big rocks.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Can you stop this boat from rocking for a minute? PHOENIX: No. We’re floating on water. I can’t do that.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Well, since you live on the water, aren’t you afraid of great white sharks?

transcript.speaker: PHOENIX
transcript.text: No, not really. They don’t live in these waters.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: … that you know of. What about killer whales?

transcript.speaker: PHOENIX
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Electric eels?

transcript.speaker: PHOENIX
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Barracudas?

transcript.speaker: PHOENIX
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Piranhas?

transcript.speaker: PHOENIX
transcript.text: Uh-uh.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Oh, oh yeah, Fanny. I have battled the great waters before -- once on a swan boat and once in a duck boat ... bus. It was a boat that turned into a bus.

transcript.speaker: FANNY
transcript.text: Yeah, I don’t think that counts.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Fanny, does this rocking ever bother you?

transcript.speaker: FANNY

transcript.text: Anna, are you feeling okay?

transcript.speaker: ANNA

mainVideo.title: Let’s Learn English - Level 2 - Lesson 28: For the Birds

transcript.speaker: KELLY
transcript.text: Oh, Anna, there you are! I am so glad we joined the Great City Bird Count! Aren't you?

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: No. Today has been a bust … a flop … a bummer!

transcript.speaker: KELLY
transcript.text: I’m sensing a little disappointment.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: A little?

transcript.speaker: KELLY
transcript.text: My official bird-watching form is almost full!

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: I've only seen pigeons ... lots and lots of pigeons! But I did write down some other valuable information.

transcript.speaker: KELLY
transcript.text: Did you find a bird's nest?!

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: No.
(She shows Kelly a map of ice cream trucks.)

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: I found 10 ice cream trucks in this five-block area.​ Their music seems to follow me everywhere.

transcript.speaker: KELLY
transcript.text: We're supposed to be counting birds, not ice cream trucks. This is important scientific work!

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Well, when you want ice cream, my data will be pretty important.

transcript.speaker: KELLY
transcript.text: Anna, birds are everywhere! I’m sure you’ll find something. Use your imagination! But, make sure that you put it on the official form.
(Anna walks away with her ice cream truck map.)

transcript.speaker: PROF. BOT
transcript.text: Anna was supposed to find birds, but she didn’t.

transcript.speaker: PROF. BOT
transcript.text: Kelly says, “We're supposed to be counting birds, not ice cream trucks.” To be supposed to means you are expected to do something.

transcript.speaker: PROF. BOT
transcript.text: It’s different from have to and ought to. Have to means you must do something. And ought to means you should do it but you don’t have to.

transcript.speaker: PROF. BOT
transcript.text: Keep watching for have to and ought to!
(Anna looks through binoculars but doesn't see birds. She talks to herself.)

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: No birds. Oh wait, there’s another ice cream truck! Anna, focus on birds. Aw, but that truck has my favorite flavor ... banana!

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: That man is in the way. I can’t see the price. I wonder what flavor he's getting.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Strawberry? He doesn't seem like a strawberry kind of guy.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: In fact, he doesn't seem like an ice cream truck kind of guy. That suit looks expensive.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Maybe he's a spy! You know what that means: The ice cream truck driver is a spy, too!

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Genius! It’s a perfect disguise.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: What?! The man in the suit left his briefcase at the ice cream truck!

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: I was right! He is a spy! And, he just dropped off top-secret information! I ought to do something. Something needs to be done! I need to do something.
(Anna runs to the ice cream truck and takes the briefcase.)

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: I did it! I took the spy’s briefcase!

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: What’s that?! The ice cream truck -- it’s following me! It wants the case back! I have to hide.
(She runs and hides behind a tree.)

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: This is my life now -- running, scared, alone.
(She runs to another tree.)

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: That awful music -- it’s following me everywhere!
(The man sees her at the tree.)

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: Hey! You found my briefcase.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: You caught me! I mean, I caught you!

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: Well, I just want my briefcase. All my poems are in there.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Poems? You’re a poet?

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: Well, I'm a lawyer. But I write poems, too.
(Anna gives the man his briefcase.)

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: So, you’re not a spy?

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: You look disappointed.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: No, that’s okay. It’s not your fault. Poems are nice, too. I guess.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: Well, would you like me to read my latest one?

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Why not?

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: On sunny day walks, my hand reaches for ice cream from fragaria.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: I love your poem!

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: I love ice cream.

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Me too.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: What's your favorite flavor?

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Banana.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: Well, my favorite flavor is ...

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: Strawberry!

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: How did you know that?

transcript.speaker: ANNA
transcript.text: A little bird told me.
